newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Berlin tense where westerners invade east.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Berlin tense where westerners invade east.

text.p: For many western Germans, the formerly communist east is a backward, broken, decrepit and polluted region where they would never want to live.
More than 1.4 million easterners have left for the west in the seven years since the Berlin Wall came down but precious few have moved in the other direction.

The exception to that one-way migration pattern is the Prenzlauer Berg district of east Berlin, where tensions are rising because thousands of well-heeled westerners have moved into the Bohemian quarter and displaced artists, squatters and low-income families.
"People are moving here because they think it is trendy," said Henry Braeutigam, a student who moved into the area after the fall of the Wall in 1989.

"But, as the prices rise, a lot of the alternative culture that attracted people in the first place, such as theatres and art centres, will disappear," he added. "It's a shame because the area is losing its charm."

Since German unification in 1990, some 60,000 of Prenzlauer Berg's 145,000 inhabitants have moved away and thousands of wealthy westerners -- the widely derided yuppies -- have moved into the district that straddles the government quarter Mitte and the west Berlin district of Wedding.

Tensions are rising between the newly-arrived westerners and the remaining easterners who fondly recall the cozy comforts of the defunct communist state and the pre-capitalist atmosphere in Prenzlauer Berg.
It's now yuppie versus Ossie, speculator versus squatter and posh versus poor.
LANDLORDS WANT TO DEVELOP, FORCE TENANTS OUT

Police report more fires break out in Prenzlauer Berg than in any other district in Berlin. Some are deliberately set by western property speculators who bought rundown buildings with plans of renovating them into high-priced flats.

But strong laws protected residents and the landlords were unable to force many of the low-income tenants out. Several landlords have been convicted by courts of bodily harm and other crimes in their efforts to frighten tenants away.

The sights and smells of gentrification are everywhere in Prenzlauer Berg, arguably one of the most charming sections of Berlin with turn-of-the-century architecture that survived World War Two and was spared the dismally drab post-war reconstruction that quickly spoiled much of West Berlin.

The clashes in Prenzlauer Berg between east and west are most pronounced on Kollwitz Platz, a square at the district's heart which was previously a site for revolutionary and riotous workers' rallies on May Day.

Despite graffitti that pay tribute to 111 years of May Day rallies, the former revolutionary hub is well on the way to becoming a yuppie haven, ringed with expensive, renovated studio flats and smart pavement bars and cafes.

The square is one of the most fashionable haunts of young Berliners and a "must" for tourist sight-seeing buses. Plans are in the pipeline to convert a former brewery into a cultural centre with a multiplex cinema, bars and shopping mall.
MERCS REPLACE TRABIS

Where smoky east German Trabant cars once stood, shiny Mercedes are now taking the parking spots on the district's cobblestone streets. Fashionable restaurants and pricey wine-bars are replacing the grimy, inexpensive beer haunts.

"We have had enough!" screams one protest poster. "Prenzlauer Berg should not become a playground for yuppies and Bonn bureaucrats. We have to foot the bill: rising rents, speculation and displacement, transport overload and the nightly terror of consumer culture."

Residents have protested fiercely at the noise of night-time revellers. Politicians from the Greens and reform communist Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS) that once won nearly half the votes in the district want to ban late night outdoor cafes.
"We used to be able to let the children play out in the streets without worrying," said Daniela Jakob, 26, an unemployed mother of three who grew up in the area.
"Now it's not safe with all the pubs and lots of unemployed people sitting out on the street and drinking all day."
Jakob, who lives with her mother and children in a small unkempt tenement, has seen her rent almost triple in five years from 320 marks ($180) per month to 940 marks.
"Although many of us have less money now than before, the rents never stop climbing," she said.
SQUATTERS PACKING THEIR BAGS

After unification many of the grand but decaying turn-of-the-century tenements were handed back to their former owners -- many westerners -- who had lost their property to the former communist East German state.

Others were occupied by squatters ousted from Kreuzberg, west Berlin's bohemian equivalent of Prenzlauer Berg, when a property boom began there. They painted their squats bright colours and set up impromptu art centres, bars and night clubs.
But the squatters and low-income tenants are packing their bags. Several schools, kindergartens and a children's library have closed because there are so few childen left.
"Despite all our efforts, there is no renovation strategy that completely rules out displacement," said the co-head of the district's tenants' advice service, Ulli Lautenschlaeger.

"Most residents want an up-to-date standard of living. The problem we have to solve is that many of the households are poor and they have to be able to afford the flats after modernisation," he said. ($ = 1.759 German Marks)
